title: Conversion of life
hookLine: a vow to keep changing, little by little, every day

cards: Can you promise to change? Not one thing by Friday, like a resolution on a sticky note. To keep changing, for the rest of your life, with no finish line.
That's the strange second promise a Benedictine monk makes. Right beside the vow to stay, in the same chapter of the Rule, sits a vow that sounds like its opposite. Stay put, and keep moving.
Same house, same brothers, same bells, and a heart that never settles into a groove.
The Latin is two words, conversatio morum, and it doesn't go easily into English: conversion of life, fidelity to the monastic way, turning of habits.

teach.h: TURNING AS A WAY OF LIVING.
teach.b: This isn't the one dramatic turn, the light on the road to Damascus. It's turning as a way of living: a little more each day, the way a plant keeps leaning toward a window. The Rule never pretends anyone arrives.

Near its end, Benedict calls the whole thing a little rule for beginners, written, he says, so that people can make a start. Then he points past it to scripture and the older teachers for anyone who wants more.
A rule for a whole life, and its author files it under beginner. Paul says something like this to the Romans: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind."
And to the Corinthians: "the inward man is renewed day by day." Day by day, not once. The Prologue of the Rule pictures where this leads.
At first, it admits, the road is narrow and hard. But as a person goes on, the heart grows wider, and they run the way of God's commandments.

teach.h: WHEN THOU SHALT ENLARGE MY HEART.
teach.b: It echoes a psalm: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart." So conversatio isn't guilt about not being finished. It's permission to never be finished.
Nobody has to fix a whole life by Tuesday. The task is to begin again, today, and again tomorrow. Stability keeps you in the room.
Conversatio keeps the room from going stale.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns make the promise of conversatio morum together with stability and obedience, which the Rule pictures as a daily turning rather than one dramatic turn.

practice: Look at your day as if you were a stranger watching it, and find one tiny habit that's gone stale: the first thing you reach for in the morning, a tone you use with someone, a shortcut you always take.
Pick the smallest one you'd actually change, not the biggest, and decide what you'll do instead, just for today. If you pray, offer that small turn to God.

wordCard.voice: Conversatio. The Benedictine promise to keep turning, a little each day, and never call yourself finished.

orig.note: Latin, from the Rule of Saint Benedict: the promise to keep turning one's way of life toward God.

carryVoice: Your line: always beginning. In this picture, forgetting isn't failure; it's the next start. See you tomorrow.
